phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar plosive [t] plus long open front [aː]; Māori t is unaspirated, and the macron marks vowel length.
Alveolar nasal [n] plus close-mid front [e], a short final syllable.

pronunciation.approximation: 'TAH-neh' — hold the first vowel long, keep the t soft and unaspirated, and pronounce the final e as a clear 'eh.'

kin.label: Proto-Polynesian
kin.form: *tane — the reconstructed common noun for 'man, male, husband' (Tregear, The Māori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary)

kin.label: Hawaiian
kin.form: Kāne — the great Hawaiian creator god, his direct cognate, one of the primordial gods of the island pantheon (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology)

kin.label: Tahitian
kin.form: Ta'ane — the Tahitian form, patron of beauty and craftsmanship in Henry's account (Henry, Ancient Tahiti)

pronunciation.note: Tāne is one of the simplest and oldest theonyms in the corpus: a Proto-Polynesian common noun for 'man' or 'male' elevated to divine status. The macron on ā marks the long vowel that distinguishes the name in Māori. Tier 1: the single long vowel is the distinctive prosodic feature preserved in the Unicode restoration.

domains.title: Forests, Birds, First Man
domains.subtitle: Creator, Separator, and Ancestor
domains.lead: Tāne is the forest made conscious, the bird made ancestor, and the man made god. In Māori cosmology he is the child who separated earth and sky, the father of humankind who shaped the first woman from clay, and the lord of every tree and winged thing. He stands at the axis of nature and culture, the one who makes space for life by pushing upward.

cards.name: Separator of Earth and Sky
cards.desc: He pushed Ranginui upward with his legs, creating the space in which the world exists.

cards.name: Lord of Forests and Birds
cards.desc: Tāne-mahuta rules the trees and all creatures that live among them, especially birds.

cards.name: Creator of Humankind
cards.desc: He formed the first woman, Hineahuone, from red clay at Kurawaka and breathed life into her nostrils.

cards.name: Seeker of Knowledge
cards.desc: He climbed through the layered heavens to obtain the three baskets of knowledge for humankind.

symbols.name: Kauri tree
symbols.meaning: The great forest tree most closely identified with Tāne-mahuta, the lord of the forest

symbols.name: Birds and feathers
symbols.meaning: Creatures of the forest canopy and markers of sacred prestige, especially the huia and kiwi

symbols.name: Red clay
symbols.meaning: The substance from which Tāne shaped the first woman, Hineahuone

symbols.name: The three baskets of knowledge
symbols.meaning: The repositories of ritual, memory, and cosmic understanding brought down from the heavens

symbols.name: Tōtara and rātā, the forest's spine
symbols.meaning: The great canopy trees whose trunks stand between earth and sky like his legs still holding them apart

mythology.lead: Tāne's myths are central to Māori cosmogony. He is the active principle of separation, the ancestor of humankind, and the culture hero who brings knowledge from the sky. The narratives are preserved in nineteenth-century written versions of oral tradition.

myths.title: The One Who Pushed the Sky
myths.text: Tāne was born in the darkness between Ranginui and Papatūānuku, and it was he who ended it. His brother Tūmatauenga urged killing their parents; Rongo, Tangaroa, and Haumia-tiketike tried and failed to force them apart. Then Tāne lay on his back between the two great bodies and pressed upward with his legs — and Ranginui rose into the sky, and the space between became the world, and light came in. The recitations linger on the aftermath: Rangi's tears falling as rain, Papa's mist rising to meet him, and the new order's first casualty — the broken embrace. Tāwhirimātea, refusing the separation, made war from the sky; it was Tāne who had to live with what his success cost. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1.) The myth's insight is that creation is violent even when no one is killed: to make room is to amputate an embrace.

myths.title: The Making of Hineahuone
myths.text: Tāne sought a companion and found none among the gods, so he made one from the earth. At Kurawaka — the place where Papatūānuku's female essence was understood to be concentrated — he took the red ochre clay and shaped it into the form of a woman: Hineahuone, 'Earth-formed woman.' Then he pressed his nose to hers in the hongi and breathed his own breath into her nostrils, and she woke, and the first couple stood together in the new world. Their daughter was Hinetītama, the dawn-maiden, and from her the whole human line descends. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology; Best, Māori Religion and Mythology.) The myth makes humanity a collaboration of body and breath — clay from the mother, spirit from the father — and locates the first birth at the earth's most emphatically female place.

myths.title: The Daughter Who Became Night
myths.text: Hinetītama grew and married the great provider of the world — and then learned, from the murmuring of the forest creatures, that her husband was her own father, Tāne. Shattered, she fled the world of light and went down into the darkness, becoming Hine-nui-te-pō, 'Great woman of the night,' the guardian of the dead. Tāne followed her to the underworld's edge and pleaded for her return; her answer — that she would keep the dead, and that her descendants would come to her one by one — is the myth's explanation of mortality. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology; White, The Ancient History of the Māori I.) It is among the starkest incest-and-exile narratives in world myth, and its result is the kindest possible death: a goddess who was wronged keeps the door, and every mortal goes home to her.

myths.title: The Ascent for the Baskets of Knowledge
myths.text: To make human life more than survival, Tāne climbed through the layered heavens — the whare-wānanga teachings count them variously, and their pre-contact antiquity is honestly debated — passing the guardian of each sky until he reached the hidden realm of Io. From Io's court he descended with the three baskets of knowledge: one holding ritual and incantation, one the memory of the ancestors and tribal tradition, one spiritual understanding; the priestly schools preserved variant names for each basket, faithfully recorded by Smith from different teaching lines. His return made learning possible and founded the authority of those who keep it. (Smith, The Lore of the Whare-wānanga; Best, The Māori School of Learning.) Knowledge, on this charter, is not discovered but fetched — a perilous ascent whose fruit is communal, carried down in baskets, by a god who climbed.

lore.syncretism: Tāne's name is one of the oldest in the corpus: Proto-Polynesian *tane, the common word for 'man,' raised to divinity. Eastward it becomes the Hawaiian Kāne, the great creator god of the island pantheon, and the Tahitian Ta'ane, patron of beauty and craftsmanship. The western islands divided the forest-and-craft domains differently — Tonga and Samoa know Tangaloa there, a name the Māori keep separately as Tangaroa, lord of the sea — so in Aotearoa Tāne absorbed portfolios that other Polynesian cultures assigned elsewhere. Contemporary Māori spirituality, environmentalism, and the arts invoke Tāne-mahuta as the living forest and the ancestor of indigenous ecological knowledge; the Māori Marsden tradition reads his separation of the parents as the primordial act by which structure, and therefore meaning, entered the cosmos.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tāne is one of the most widely known Māori deities, especially through the famous kauri tree named Tāne Mahuta in Waipoua Forest, a major spiritual site visited by thousands each year. His image appears in carving, painting, dance, and environmental advocacy throughout Aotearoa. The story of the separation of Rangi and Papa is taught in schools as a founding narrative, and Tāne's quest for knowledge informs contemporary discussions of Māori education and intellectual tradition — the whare-wānanga, the Māori university colleges, bear the name of the very schools whose lore his myth charters. He has become an emblem of the living forest in an age of deforestation and climate change: to defend the ngahere, the forest, is to defend his body.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Tāne begins as a word for 'man' and becomes the god who makes the world spacious enough to live in. That trajectory is itself a meditation on masculinity: not the masculinity of domination, but of upward pressure, of making room, of separating so that others can breathe. He does not kill his father; he lifts him. He does not abandon his mother; he stays beneath her, supporting life upon her body.

The first woman is made of clay and animated by breath — a myth that echoes across many cultures but finds a particularly tactile form here. Tāne shapes, then he breathes; and the making of people is thus a double inheritance, body from the mother-earth and breath from the father-sky. Knowledge is not innate either; it must be climbed for, through successive heavens, with effort and guardianship. The name Tāne, short and long-voweled, holds all of this: the man who is also the forest, the ancestor who is also the sky, the maker of room in a world that began with none.

lore.archaeology: As with Papatūānuku, Tāne's primary preservation is oral and environmental rather than monumental — no temple was built to him, because the forest was the temple. The Waipoua kauri forest in Northland contains the tree named Tāne Mahuta, one of the largest and oldest living kauri, a natural shrine; the rātā and tōtara forests of the islands were managed as his body under customary regimes that fused religion and conservation. Māori wharenui, waka taua (war canoes), and carving invoke him through tree and bird imagery — the house itself is his standing form, ridge-beam as spine, posts as limbs. The nineteenth-century records of Grey, Best, White, and Smith remain the principal textual witnesses, taken down while the whare-wānanga schools still taught the full cycle.
